cards.q: What does filtering control in redistribution and which tools are used?
cards.a: Filtering decides which routes cross the redistribution boundary. Blind redistribution creates loops, black holes, and metric surprises. The tools are route-maps (the modern standard), distribute-lists, and prefix-lists, applied at the boundary router on the redistributing protocol.

cards.q: Where are redistribution filters placed and in which direction do they run?
cards.a: Filters run at the boundary router, before routes enter the receiving protocol, using route-maps on the redistribute command, distribute-lists (EIGRP in/out; OSPF in only), or prefix-lists matched inside a route-map.

cards.q: How does a route-map filter and set metrics during redistribution?
cards.a: A route-map matches prefixes with a prefix-list and sets the metric (e.g., set metric 10000 100 255 1 1500), applied to redistribute. Only matched prefixes redistribute; everything else is dropped by the implicit deny.

cards.q: What is the role of the implicit deny at the end of a route-map?
cards.a: Non-matched routes are dropped by the implicit deny at the end of a route-map, so only the prefixes explicitly matched by a permit statement redistribute.

cards.q: How do distribute-lists 'in' and 'out' directions work?
cards.a: The 'in' filter filters routes received, and 'out' filters routes sent, on the local router. OSPF only supports 'in' on Cisco IOS.

cards.q: What is the difference between filtering at redistribution versus filtering to a BGP neighbor?
cards.a: 'redistribute ospf ... route-map RM' filters what enters EIGRP locally, while 'neighbor ... route-map RM out' filters what leaves to a BGP peer. The in/out direction is on the local router, not the neighbor — misplacing the direction lets routes slip through.

cards.q: What are the goals of filtering in redistribution and the matching methods?
cards.a: Loop prevention (deny own-origin prefixes back in), keeping the table small (advertise only needed prefixes), avoiding feedback (deny tagged routes), controlling MED (route-map set metric), and policy at the edge (prefix-list/as-path).

cards.q: Which commands verify filtered routes and route-map counters?
cards.a: 'show route-map' shows counters, 'show ip prefix-list' shows ACL state, 'show ip eigrp topology' shows absence of blocked routes, and 'debug ip routing' traces.

cards.q: Why does OSPF only support the distribute-list 'in' direction on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: Because of how OSPF builds its best-path tree on interfaces; on Cisco IOS OSPF distribute-list is restricted to filtering received/interface-based routes (in) only, not outgoing.

cards.q: What is the strongest loop defense in redistribution filtering?
cards.a: Tag-based denies — filter routes already carrying a loop-prevention tag so they never return to their origin protocol.

cards.q: Too many routes are being redistributed. What could be the cause and check?
cards.a: A missing filter or wrong filter direction; check 'show ip protocols' and the direction of the route-map/distribute-list.

cards.q: A redistributed route is missing even though it should pass. What is the likely cause?
cards.a: The filter is too strict — the route-map or prefix-list is not matching the prefix; check 'show route-map' counters and 'show ip prefix-list detail'.

cards.q: In the filtering quick review, what are the key tools and behaviors?
cards.a: Standard approach is a route-map on redistribute; alternative is distribute-list; selector is prefix-list/ACL; OSPF is distribute in only; direction is local in/out; implicit deny at the end; loop fix via tag-based deny; verify with show route-map.
